## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.105734.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.105734.3.sa2)

Summary:

The current study aims to shed light on why previous work on perceptual rhythmicity has led to inconsistent results. They propose that the differences may stem from conceptual and methodological issues. In a series of experiments, the current study reports perceptual rhythmicity in different frequency bands that differ between different ear stimulations and behavioral measures. The study suggests challenges regarding the idea of universal perceptual rhythmicity in hearing.

Strengths:

The study aims to address differences observed in previous studies about perceptual rhythmicity. This is important and timely because the existing literature provides quite inconsistent findings. Several experiments were conducted to assess perceptual rhythmicity in hearing from different angles. The authors use sophisticated approaches to address the research questions. The manuscript has greatly improved after the revision.

Weaknesses:

Additional variance: In several experiments, a fixation cross preceded - at a variable interval - the onset of the background noise that aimed to reset the phase of an ongoing oscillation. There is the chance that the fixation cross also resets the phase, potentially adding variance to the data. In addition, the authors used an adaptive procedure during the experimental blocks such that the stimulus intensity was adjusted throughout. There is good reason for doing so, but it means that correctly identified/discriminated targets will on average have a greater stimulus intensity. This may add variance to the data. These two aspects may potentially contribute to the observation of weak perceptual rhythmicity.

Figures: The text in Figures 4 and 6 is small. I think readers would benefit from a larger font size. Moreover, Figure 1A is not very intuitive. Perhaps it could be made clearer. The new Figure 5 was not discussed in the text. I wonder whether analyses with traditional t-tests could be placed in the supplements.

50% significant samples: The authors consider 50% of significant bootstrapped samples robust. For example: "This revealed that the above‐mentioned effects prevail for at least 50% of the simulated experiments, corroborating their robustness within the participant sample". Many of the effects have even lower than 50% of significant samples. It is a matter of opinion of what is robust or not, but I think combined with the overall variable nature of the effects in different frequency bands and ears etc. leaves more the impression that the effects are not very robust. I think the authors state it correctly in the last sentence of the first paragraph of the discussion: "At the same time the prevalence of significant effects in random samples of participants were mostly below 50%, raising questions as to the ubiquity of such effects." I think the authors should update the abstract in this regard to avoid that readers who only read the abstract get the wrong impression about the robustness of the effects. It is not clear to me if the same study (using the same conditions) was done in a different lab that the results would come out similarly to the results reported here.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.105734.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.105734.3.sa3)

Summary:

The finding of rhythmic activity in the brain has for a long time engendered the theory of rhythmic modes of perception, that humans might oscillate between improved and worse perception depending on states of our internal systems. However, experiments looking for such modes have resulted in conflicting findings, particularly in those where the stimulus itself is not rhythmic. This paper seeks to take a comprehensive look at the effect and various experimental parameters which might generate these competing findings: in particular, the presentation of the stimulus to one ear or the other, the relevance of motor involvement, attentional demands, and memory: each of which are revealed to effect the consistency of this rhythmicity.

The need the paper attempts to resolve is a critical one for the field. However, as presented, I remain unconvinced that the data would not be better interpreted as showing no consistent rhythmic mode effect.

Strengths:

The paper is strong in its experimental protocol and its comprehensive analysis which seeks to compare effects across several analysis types and slight experiment changes to investigate which parameters could effect the presence or absence of an effect of rhythmicity. The prescribed nature of its hypotheses and its manner to set out to test them is very clear which allows for a straightforward assessment of its results

Weaknesses:

The papers cited to justify a rhythmic mode are largely based on the processing of rhythmic stimuli. The authors assume the rhythmic mode to be the general default but its not so clear to me why this would be so. The task design seems better suited to a continuous vigilance mode task.

Secondly, the analysis to detect a "rhythmic mode", assumes a total phase rest at noise onset which is highly implausible given standard nonlinear dynamical analysis of oscillator performance. It's not clear that a rhythmic mode (should it be applied in this task) would indeed generate a consistent phase as the analysis searches for.

Thirdly, the number of statistical tests used here make trusting any single effect quite difficult and very few of the effects replicate more than once. I think the better would be interpreted as not confirming evidence for rhythmic mode processing in the ears.

Comments on revised version:

No further comments. The paper has much of the same issues that I expressed in the initial review but I don't think they can be addressed without a replication study which I appreciate is not always plausible.

results.result: Previous literature on rhythmic auditory perception shows inconsistent evidence, which the authors attribute to conceptual and methodological issues including ambiguous assumptions about the origin of rhythmicity, variations in tasks and attentional demands, and differing analytical approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C21-C23 collectively establish the motivation for the study by documenting inconsistencies in prior work and proposing explanations. These are well-supported by citations to previous literature and represent a reasonable synthesis of the field's state.

results.result: Four experiments were conducted with monaural auditory targets presented against binaural white noise, varying in trial pacing (automatic vs. manual initialization), memory requirements (between-trial vs. within-trial discrimination), and attentional demands (single vs. dual task). Eye movements were recorded in Experiment 4. Sample sizes ranged from 26-36 participants across experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7, C27, C30-C35, and C82-C103 provide comprehensive methodological details that are internally consistent and appropriately documented. The experimental design is clearly described with adequate sample sizes and proper ethical approval.

results.result: Three analytical approaches were developed and calibrated using simulated data: spectral analysis of binned data, linear model analysis of binned data, and linear model analysis of single-trial data. False positive rates were calibrated to ~0.05 across approaches. Bootstrapping was used to assess effect prevalence across participant samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 and C104-C119 describe a rigorous analytical framework with appropriate calibration procedures. The use of simulations to equate false positive rates across methods and bootstrapping to assess generalizability represents sound statistical practice.

results.result: Behavioral data showed temporal structure with decreasing sensitivity and reaction times for targets presented late in trials, consistent with previous perceptual decision-making studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 describe general temporal trends in the data that are supported by visual inspection (Figure 3) and are consistent with cited prior work. These represent expected patterns in perceptual decision-making tasks.

results.result: Statistical analysis revealed significant rhythmic effects in specific experiments: d-prime at ~2 Hz for right ear in Experiment 1, bias at ~6.5 Hz for left ear in Experiment 2, and d-prime at ~3 Hz for combined-ear data in Experiment 3. These effects prevailed in at least 50% of resampled participant samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 report statistically significant effects, but the prevalence of only 50% in resampled data raises questions about robustness. The effects differ substantially across experiments that vary in task demands, making it unclear whether these represent genuine rhythmic perception or task-specific artifacts.

results.result: Prevalence analysis across experiments revealed that multiple behavioral metrics (sensitivity, bias) show rhythmicity at comparable rates across experiments and ears, but the precise frequencies and prevalence vary between analytical approaches and experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 acknowledge substantial heterogeneity in results across methods and experiments. While the prevalence analysis is methodologically sound (C117-C119), the inconsistency in frequencies and metrics across experiments undermines confidence in a unified rhythmic mechanism. The prevalence values are often below 50%, questioning the generalizability of effects.

results.result: Averaged across experiments, the two ears exhibited rhythmic effects at complementary frequencies (right ear: ~2 Hz and 4 Hz; left ear: ~3 Hz and 6 Hz). Correlation analysis showed minimal co-occurrence of effects between ears (r≈0, p>0.2), suggesting rhythmicity in left and right ears may emerge in separate groups of participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59 propose ear-specific rhythmicity at different frequencies, supported by averaged prevalence data (C54-C56) and correlation analysis (C58). However, the lack of correlation between ears (C58-C59) and the averaging across experiments with different task demands raises questions about whether this represents a stable phenomenon or statistical noise. The interpretation requires replication.

results.result: In Experiment 4, participants performed well on the dual visual task (d-prime=3.96±0.12). The dual task increased reaction times and altered bias but not sensitivity to tones. Direct comparison showed no significant difference in rhythmicity between dual-task and single-task conditions for the specific sample, but prevalence analysis suggested ~40% of participants showed stronger rhythmicity at 4 Hz and 8 Hz during dual-task conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C67 present mixed evidence for dual-task effects. While participants performed the dual task well (C60-C61) and it affected some behavioral measures (C62-C63), the lack of significant group-level differences (C65) combined with modest prevalence effects (C66-C67) provides only weak support for attention-dependent rhythmicity. The interpretation that a 'subgroup' shows effects (C67) is speculative.

results.result: Pupil size showed no relationship with rhythmicity in behavior. However, trials with less fixation stability (more eye mobility) showed significantly stronger rhythmic effects for sensitivity around 3.5 Hz (prevalence 64%), suggesting rhythmicity is more expressed when eye mobility is larger. This effect likely relates to microsaccades or drifts rather than overt saccades (average 0.79±0.1 saccades/trial).
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C74 provide clear evidence distinguishing pupil effects (absent) from fixation stability effects (present). The statistical significance (C70), high prevalence (C71), and characterization of eye movements (C73-C74) support the conclusion that oculomotor activity relates to rhythmicity. This represents one of the more robust findings in the study.

results.result: Task difficulty was maintained at similar levels throughout experiments by adaptively adjusting stimulus parameters. Group-level stimulus parameters did not differ significantly between start and end of Experiments 1, 2, and 4.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 document appropriate experimental control to prevent confounding by learning or fatigue. Statistical tests confirm no systematic changes in difficulty (C76), supporting the validity of pooling data across trial time.

results.result: The findings challenge universal rhythmicity in hearing but support paradigm- and ear-specific fluctuations in sensitivity and biases at multiple frequencies. Rhythmicity for left and right ears appears independent among participants and may be linked to oculomotor activity and attentional requirements. The authors conclude against mandatory rhythmicity governing auditory perception per se, instead proposing that multiple processes (temporal entrainment, neural adaptation, predictive processes, motor-related processes) interact to shape perception in paradigm-specific ways.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 and C77-C81 represent the main conclusions but are only partially supported by the data. While the study demonstrates task-dependent variability and links to oculomotor behavior (supporting C9, C11, C78-C79), the evidence against universal rhythmicity (C8, C77) is based largely on inconsistency across experiments rather than definitive null results. The mechanistic speculation (C80-C81) goes beyond the data. The low prevalence of effects (<50% in many cases) and lack of replication across experiments limit confidence in the positive claims.

results.result: The authors review theoretical frameworks for rhythmic perception, including perceptual cycles, the alignment of neural rhythms with speech structure, and the distinction between rhythmic and continuous listening modes. They note that rhythmicity could originate from monaural processes operating at different frequencies per ear or from higher-level cognitive processes operating uniformly across ears.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C20 and C24-C29 accurately summarize prior theoretical and empirical work with appropriate citations. These provide necessary context for the study's design and interpretation, representing a fair characterization of the literature.

results.result: The manuscript reviews the literature on rhythmic perception in hearing, noting that while numerous studies advocate for rhythmic modes of perception, the evidence remains inconsistent, with some studies reporting positive results and others finding weak or no evidence for rhythmicity.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge this characterization of the literature. Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'The first sentence in the abstract describes the state of the art perfectly' and notes this is 'precisely why the data from the present study is so valuable.' The editor describes the work as addressing 'rhythmicity in behavioral performance during listening' without challenging the premise.

results.result: The authors propose that divergent conclusions in previous work stem from conceptual and methodological issues, including ambiguous assumptions about the origin of rhythmicity, variations in tasks and attentional demands, and differing analytical approaches.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this framing. Reviewer 2 states the study 'aims to shed light on why previous work on perceptual rhythmicity has led to inconsistent results' and that 'the study aims to address differences observed in previous studies about perceptual rhythmicity. This is important and timely.' No reviewer challenges this premise.

results.result: The study conducted four experiments with monaural targets presented against binaural white noise backgrounds while recording eye movements. The experiments systematically varied motor initialization requirements, memory demands, and attentional requirements through dual-task manipulations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praise the experimental design. Reviewer 1 notes 'Each of the experiments differs from the others in a clearly defined experimental parameter' and Reviewer 3 states 'The paper is strong in its experimental protocol.' The editor describes it as a 'high-N, multi-task study' that 'offers a comprehensive examination.' No concerns are raised about the experimental design itself.

results.result: The authors simulated data with and without rhythmicity to calibrate three statistical approaches (spectra-based, binned data analysis, and single-trial analysis), determining thresholds that result in a false-positive rate of approximately 0.05.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly praises 'the comparison of several statistical approaches and simulations of their sensitivity,' noting 'The analysis is very thorough and transparent.' No reviewer challenges the validity of this methodological calibration approach.

results.result: Across experiments 1-3, the authors found significant rhythmic effects at different frequencies for different ears and behavioral metrics: experiment 1 showed effects around 2 Hz for the right ear and 6.5 Hz for the left ear; experiment 2 showed effects around 6.5 Hz for the left ear; experiment 3 showed effects around 2-3 Hz for combined-ear data. These effects prevailed in at least 50% of bootstrapped samples.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express significant concerns about the robustness and interpretation of these findings. Reviewer 2 critically notes that 'Many of the effects have even lower than 50% of significant samples' and questions whether 'the same study (using the same conditions) was done in a different lab that the results would come out similarly.' Reviewer 1 states 'it remains to be shown whether there is any systematic pattern in the results that allows conclusions about the roles of different frequencies.' Reviewer 3 states 'I remain unconvinced that the data would not be better interpreted as showing no consistent rhythmic mode effect' and notes 'very few of the effects replicate more than once.'

results.result: The findings challenge the notion of universal rhythmicity in hearing, instead supporting paradigm-specific effects that pertain to sensitivity or response biases independently and may emerge at different frequencies for each ear.
results.evaluation: Reviewers have mixed views on this conclusion. The editor states the work presents 'valuable findings that reveal task- and ear-specific effects, challenging the notion of a universal rhythmicity in auditory perception' and calls the evidence 'solid.' However, Reviewer 3 states 'I remain unconvinced that the data would not be better interpreted as showing no consistent rhythmic mode effect' and suggests 'the better would be interpreted as not confirming evidence for rhythmic mode processing in the ears.' Reviewer 2 notes concerns about robustness that should be reflected in the abstract.

results.result: Multiple behavioral metrics reveal comparable prevalence of rhythmicity across experiments and ears, with the two ears tending to exhibit effects at complementary frequencies: right ear peaks around 2 Hz and 4 Hz, left ear peaks around 3 Hz and 6 Hz. However, precise frequencies and prevalence vary between approaches and experiments.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes this variability as a weakness: 'it remains to be shown whether there is any systematic pattern in the results that allows conclusions about the roles of different frequencies' and questions 'whether they merely reflect some natural variability (independent of experimental parameters) or are indeed driven by the specific experimental paradigm (and therefore replicable).' Reviewer 2 notes 'the overall variable nature of the effects in different frequency bands and ears etc. leaves more the impression that the effects are not very robust.'

results.result: The rhythmicity for sounds in the left and right ears appears independent among participants, with minimal correlations (r≈0) in the co-occurrence of effects between ears, suggesting rhythmicity may emerge in separate groups of participants rather than simultaneously.
results.evaluation: No reviewer directly challenges this finding. The editor acknowledges 'ear-specific effects' as part of the valuable findings. While reviewers question the overall robustness of rhythmicity effects, they do not specifically dispute the independence of left and right ear effects.

results.result: Rhythmicity in performance is possibly linked to oculomotor activity, with trials showing less fixation stability exhibiting significantly stronger rhythmic effects around 3.5 Hz (64% prevalence). The influence appears linked to microsaccadic behavior or drifts rather than overt saccades.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenges this finding. Reviewer 3 acknowledges the study investigates 'the relevance of motor involvement' as one of the experimental parameters. The finding is presented as exploratory and the authors appropriately qualify it as 'possibly linked,' which reviewers do not dispute.

results.result: A dual-task manipulation (experiment 4) significantly affected reaction times and bias but not sensitivity to tone frequencies. Direct statistical comparison revealed no significant difference for combined-ear data, though prevalence analysis suggested a subgroup of participants exhibited more rhythmicity at 4 Hz and 8 Hz during the dual task.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenges these specific findings from experiment 4. Reviewer 3 acknowledges the study examines 'attentional demands' as a parameter. The weak effects are consistent with reviewers' overall concerns about robustness but are not specifically disputed.

results.result: No significant relationship was found between pupil dilation and rhythmicity in auditory performance, with very low prevalence of significant effects in bootstrapped samples.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenges this null finding. It is presented as a negative control and reviewers do not dispute it.

results.result: The authors speculate that multiple processes including temporal entrainment, neural adaptation, temporally predictive processes, and motor-related processes interact to shape auditory perception, and that specific paradigms tap into unique combinations of perceptual and motor requirements, potentially explaining the diversity of previous results.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises conceptual concerns about the theoretical framework, stating 'The papers cited to justify a rhythmic mode are largely based on the processing of rhythmic stimuli' and questioning 'its not so clear to me why this would be so. The task design seems better suited to a continuous vigilance mode task.' This suggests the theoretical interpretation may not be fully supported by the experimental design.

results.result: Behavioral data showed temporal structure including decreasing sensitivity and reaction times for targets presented late in trials, consistent with previous studies on perceptual decision-making paradigms.
results.evaluation: No reviewer challenges this observation. It is presented as a general feature of the data consistent with known phenomena in decision-making tasks.

results.result: Task difficulty was maintained at a similar level throughout experiments by adaptively adjusting stimulus parameters. At the group level, parameters did not differ systematically between the start and end of experiments 1, 2, and 4.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises concerns about this adaptive procedure: 'the authors used an adaptive procedure during the experimental blocks such that the stimulus intensity was adjusted throughout. There is good reason for doing so, but it means that correctly identified/discriminated targets will on average have a greater stimulus intensity. This may add variance to the data' and suggests 'These two aspects may potentially contribute to the observation of weak perceptual rhythmicity.'

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the characterization of inconsistent literature (C1, C2, C21-C23). OpenEval notes this represents a reasonable synthesis; peer reviewers explicitly praise this framing as 'perfect' and 'precisely why the data is valuable.'

Both support the study's motivation regarding inconsistent results (C3, C4). OpenEval includes these in broader literature synthesis; peer reviewers specifically endorse this as 'important and timely' without challenge.

Both strongly support the experimental design and methodology (C5-C7, C27, C30-C35). OpenEval finds methods comprehensive and internally consistent; peer reviewers praise the 'clearly defined experimental parameters' and 'strong experimental protocol.'

Both support the analytical calibration approach (C36-C38). OpenEval describes it as rigorous statistical practice; peer reviewer 1 explicitly praises 'the comparison of several statistical approaches and simulations' as 'thorough and transparent.'
Perfect agreement on general temporal trends (C39-C41). Both accept these as expected patterns in decision-making tasks; no reviewer challenges these observations.

Both express uncertainty about robustness of rhythmicity effects (C42-C44, C47). OpenEval notes 50% prevalence raises robustness questions; peer reviewers critically note 'many effects have lower than 50% significant samples' and question replicability across labs.

Both uncertain about heterogeneity across experiments (C48-C51). OpenEval notes inconsistency undermines confidence in unified mechanism; peer reviewers state 'variable nature of effects leaves impression that effects are not very robust.'

Both uncertain about frequency-specific patterns (C52-C53). OpenEval acknowledges substantial heterogeneity; peer reviewer 1 questions 'whether there is any systematic pattern' versus 'natural variability.'

Both uncertain about ear-specific rhythmicity (C54-C56). OpenEval questions stability of averaged prevalence data; peer reviewers note 'variable nature of effects in different frequency bands and ears' suggests lack of robustness.
OpenEval uncertain about ear independence (C57-C59) requiring replication; peer reviewers support this finding without direct challenge, acknowledging 'ear-specific effects' as valuable.

Both uncertain about dual-task effects (C60-C67). OpenEval notes weak support with modest prevalence; peer reviewers accept findings but don't specifically dispute the weak effects, consistent with overall robustness concerns.

Both support fixation stability findings (C68-C74). OpenEval describes this as one of the most robust findings with high prevalence; peer reviewers acknowledge investigation of 'motor involvement' without challenge.
Both support pupil null finding (C68-C69). OpenEval and peer reviewers accept this as appropriate negative control without dispute.

Disagreement on experimental control (C75-C76). OpenEval supports the adaptive procedure as appropriate control; peer reviewer 2 raises concerns that adaptive adjustment 'may add variance to the data' and 'potentially contribute to weak perceptual rhythmicity.'

Both uncertain about main conclusions (C8, C77-C79). OpenEval notes evidence against universal rhythmicity based on inconsistency rather than definitive nulls; peer reviewers mixed—editor calls evidence 'solid' but reviewer 3 suggests data 'better interpreted as showing no consistent rhythmic mode effect.'

Both uncertain about mechanistic speculation (C80-C81). OpenEval states speculation 'goes beyond the data'; peer reviewer 3 questions theoretical framework, noting cited papers 'largely based on processing of rhythmic stimuli' while task 'seems better suited to continuous vigilance mode.'

OpenEval supports literature review claims (C12-C20, C24-C29) as fair characterization with appropriate citations. No corresponding specific peer evaluation found, though peer reviewers generally accept the literature framing.

OpenEval supports detailed analytical framework including calibration, simulations, and bootstrapping (C104-C119) as sound statistical practice. While peer reviewer 1 praises the approach generally (R4), no peer evaluation specifically addresses these detailed methodological claims.
